name: GRE-tier General
description: Genuinely useful advanced words — the ones that earn their place in real writing, not the ones that only appear on tests.

entries.definition: Present everywhere at once, to the point of being unremarkable.
examples: Short-form video is ubiquitous now, which means it's a baseline capability and not a strategy.
The greenscreen-reaction format went from novel to ubiquitous in about eleven months.
Anything ubiquitous stops being a differentiator the moment it stops being scarce.
entries.note: The useful implication for strategy writing: ubiquity and advantage are opposites. If everyone has it, it's table stakes.

entries.definition: Judging by what works rather than by what ought to work in principle.
examples: The pragmatic call is to keep the ugly landing page that converts and rebuild it next quarter.
Pragmatism becomes a problem when it's used to avoid ever fixing anything structural.
There's a pragmatic version of every ideal and it usually ships six months sooner.
entries.note: Careful — “let's be pragmatic” is often a rhetorical move to end a debate rather than an argument. Notice when it's being used on you.

entries.definition: Lasting a very short time by nature — not failing to last, but built not to.
examples: Stories are ephemeral by design, and that's exactly why they get more honest engagement than the grid.
A viral moment is ephemeral; a creator relationship is the asset it should be converted into.
Ephemeral content is cheap to make and worthless to archive, which is a fair trade if you know it going in.
entries.note: Not a synonym for “brief” — the shortness is intrinsic. A meeting is short; a mayfly is ephemeral.

entries.definition: Changing suddenly and without discernible reason.
examples: The algorithm isn't capricious, it just optimizes for something we can't see — but it's rational to plan as though it were.
A capricious client is more expensive than a demanding one, because you can't build a process around them.
Treating a system as capricious is a decision to stop trying to model it.
entries.note: Implies arbitrariness, not just volatility. Reserve it for things that change without a reason, not things that change unpredictably.

entries.definition: Stripped of ornament — plain to the point of severity, whether by taste or by necessity.
examples: The austere version of the deck is eight slides and one number per slide, and it lands harder than the forty-slide one.
Austere design is confident design; it has nothing to hide behind.
An austere budget forces the prioritization a comfortable one lets you avoid.
entries.note: Applies to aesthetics, budgets, and personalities. In design contexts it's a compliment; in personal ones it usually isn't.

entries.definition: According to what's claimed, with the implication that the truth may differ.
examples: The partnership is ostensibly about distribution; in practice it's about them getting a look at our retention data.
The meeting was ostensibly a check-in and was actually a decision meeting nobody labeled.
Ostensibly is a polite way to raise an eyebrow in print.
entries.note: It plants doubt without accusing anyone. Powerful in a memo, and slightly passive-aggressive — use once, deliberately.

entries.definition: Understood without being stated — real, agreed, and never written down.
examples: There's a tacit rule on the team that nobody posts on a Friday, and it's cost us two good launch windows.
Tacit knowledge is the reason a new hire takes three months: the doc explains the process, not the exceptions.
Every tacit agreement becomes a problem the first time someone new joins.
entries.note: The organizational insight worth a post: what a company hasn't written down is usually the part that actually runs it.

entries.definition: Just coming into existence — real but not yet formed.
examples: There's a nascent community in the comment section of three of our creators, and it will either be cultivated or it will move to Discord without us.
Nascent markets reward presence over polish.
The nascent version of any category looks like a hobby right up until it doesn't.
entries.note: Carries optimism that “early” doesn't — nascent implies the thing is genuinely forming, not just underdeveloped.

entries.definition: Focused on the near term at the cost of seeing what's coming.
examples: Optimizing every video for day-one views is myopic; the library is worth more than any single upload.
Myopic decisions are usually rational under a short measurement window, which is why the window is the real problem.
The cure for myopia in a team is almost always a longer reporting period.
entries.note: Best used about incentives rather than people. “The metric is myopic” lands; “you're myopic” starts a fight.

entries.definition: Right about what was coming, before there was evidence for it.
examples: The prescient call was staffing creators in 2023 when the whole industry was still buying installs at auction.
Prescience is indistinguishable from luck for about two years, and then it isn't.
Everyone is prescient in retrospect, which is why written predictions with dates are so valuable.
entries.note: Cheap to claim afterwards. Writing predictions down with dates is the only version of this word that means anything.

entries.definition: Resistant to solution — not merely hard, but not yielding to the approaches available.
examples: Creator burnout looked intractable until we changed the pay structure; it turned out to be a design problem wearing a human-nature costume.
Most intractable problems are tractable at a different altitude.
Label a problem intractable and you've decided to route around it, so decide that on purpose.
entries.note: A strong claim. Before writing it, ask whether the problem is genuinely intractable or just outside the current team's control.

entries.definition: Clear, logical, and convincing — an argument whose pieces actually connect.
examples: The most cogent case for the creator budget is one page: cost per funded account, by channel, over twelve months.
Cogent isn't the same as persuasive; some very persuasive arguments have no structure at all.
A cogent memo survives being forwarded to someone who wasn't in the meeting.
entries.note: The forwarding test is the best measure of cogency. If it needs you in the room to make sense, it isn't cogent yet.

entries.definition: Showy in a way designed to be noticed — display for the sake of display.
examples: There's an ostentatious way to report a good quarter and a quiet way, and the quiet way gets believed.
Ostentatious spending in a startup is a signal, and rarely the one intended.
The opposite move — understatement — costs nothing and reads as confidence.
entries.note: Direct antonym of understated. Both are choices about signaling, and the choice says more than the thing being signaled.

entries.definition: More than is needed — removable without loss.
examples: Half the slides in the QBR are superfluous; they're there because someone made them, not because anyone needs them.
Superfluous words in a memo aren't neutral — they dilute the ones that matter.
Cut anything superfluous and what's left gets louder without being longer.
entries.note: The editing test in one word: if removing it costs nothing, it was superfluous and it's gone.

entries.definition: Careful about small details, consistently and by habit.
examples: The creators who go furthest aren't the most talented, they're the most meticulous about the first three seconds.
Meticulous work is invisible when it's done and glaring when it isn't.
There's a line between meticulous and slow, and it's whether the care is going into things that matter.
entries.note: A compliment about process rather than outcome. Pairs well with “considered” from the Taste deck — same underlying value.

entries.definition: Demanding sustained effort over a long stretch — hard because it's long, not because it's complex.
examples: Recruiting 40 creators one at a time was arduous, unglamorous, and the actual reason the program works.
Arduous work is the part case studies compress into a sentence.
The arduous path is often the defensible one precisely because most people won't take it.
entries.note: Emphasizes duration and grind. A problem can be difficult without being arduous, and vice versa.

entries.definition: Using very few words — brief to the point of being striking.
examples: Jae's laconic “why?” on a Slack thread does more work than a paragraph of pushback from anyone else.
A laconic reply can read as confidence or as disdain, and the sender rarely controls which.
The most laconic line in the memo is usually the one people quote back.
entries.note: From Laconia, home of the Spartans, who were famous for it. Brevity plus a little steel — not the same as merely concise.

entries.definition: Using far more words than the content requires.
examples: The first draft of every strategy memo is verbose because writing long is how you find out what you think.
Verbose writing usually signals unfinished thinking, not excessive thinking.
Cutting a verbose paragraph in half almost never loses information.
entries.note: The right response to a verbose draft is another pass, not an apology. Length is a symptom; the disease is unresolved argument.

entries.definition: So ordinary and overfamiliar that it carries no interest at all.
examples: “Consistency is key” is banal; “post at the cadence you can sustain in your worst week” is the same idea made useful.
Banal advice survives because it's unfalsifiable and comfortable to repeat.
The gap between banal and profound is usually specificity.
entries.note: Close cousin of platitude, aimed at content rather than phrasing. The fix for both is always a concrete detail.

entries.definition: Understood only by a small group with specialized knowledge.
examples: Attribution modeling is esoteric, and translating it into one sentence a CEO can act on is most of the job.
Esoteric knowledge is valuable exactly in proportion to how few people can translate it.
Content that stays esoteric stays small; the audience is the translation.
entries.note: The core creator insight, in one word: the money is in the translation layer between esoteric knowledge and a general audience.

entries.definition: Excessively concerned with minor correctness in a way that obstructs the point.
examples: It's pedantic to correct “users” to “accounts” in a Slack message and essential to correct it in a board deck.
Pedantry is precision applied at the wrong altitude.
The distinction between pedantic and rigorous is whether the correction changes a decision.
entries.note: That last test is worth internalizing before any review comment: does this change what anyone does? If not, it's pedantry.

entries.definition: Harmless — usually said of something that could have been harmful and wasn't.
examples: An innocuous copy change on the signup screen dropped conversion 8%, which is why we test innocuous changes.
The most damaging assumptions in a plan are always the innocuous-looking ones nobody flagged.
It seemed innocuous at the time is the opening line of most postmortems.
entries.note: Almost always used ironically in a business context — the innocuous thing turned out not to be. Lean into that.

entries.definition: Superficially convincing but wrong once examined.
examples: The claim that our best creators drive retention is specious — we assign our best creators to the segments that already retain.
Specious reasoning is more dangerous than obvious nonsense because it survives the first read.
Anything that sounds right immediately deserves a second pass.
entries.note: Distinct from spurious: spurious is about a false statistical relationship, specious is about an argument that looks sound and isn't.

entries.definition: Cheerfully confident about how something will turn out, especially in a difficult situation.
examples: I'm sanguine about Q4 despite the CPM environment — the creator library carries most of the number regardless of auction prices.
Being sanguine is only useful if you can say what would change your mind.
There's a difference between sanguine and unbothered, and it's whether you've looked at the numbers.
entries.note: Slightly formal, which is why it works in a memo — it signals considered optimism rather than good mood.

entries.definition: Steadiness of mind under pressure — not calm because nothing is wrong, calm while things are.
examples: The skill in a creator program isn't taste, it's equanimity: a video flops, a creator ghosts, and Monday still needs a plan.
Equanimity is what makes a bear market survivable for an investor and a bad quarter survivable for an operator.
It's a practice, not a temperament, which is the encouraging part.
entries.note: The word for the disposition every operating role actually selects for. Good anchor for a reflective LinkedIn post.

entries.definition: Cheerful readiness — moving quickly and willingly, not just quickly.
examples: The creators who respond with alacrity get the best briefs, and everyone involved knows it.
Alacrity is speed with willingness attached; you can be fast and grudging, and people notice.
Responding with alacrity to a small request is how you get asked about the big ones.
entries.note: Formal but genuinely useful, because English is short on words that combine speed with attitude.

entries.definition: Generous toward someone you could reasonably have treated worse — especially a rival or someone who erred.
examples: The magnanimous move when a creator's exclusive deal lapses is to congratulate them publicly; the industry is small and everyone is watching.
Magnanimity in a postmortem costs nothing and buys years of goodwill.
It's only magnanimous if you had the standing to do otherwise.
entries.note: The condition matters — generosity from a position of weakness is just necessity. That's what distinguishes it from being nice.

entries.definition: To make something confusing on purpose, usually to hide what it means.
examples: Reporting “engagement up 40%” without the denominator obfuscates a flat quarter.
Fee disclosures are a masterclass in obfuscating through completeness — every fact present, nothing findable.
Complexity is sometimes honest; obfuscation never is.
entries.note: Implies intent. Confusing writing is usually a failure of drafting; obfuscation is a choice, and the accusation is serious.

entries.definition: To make an existing bad situation worse.
examples: Adding creators exacerbates the review bottleneck instead of relieving it — more input into a constrained system is just a longer queue.
The discount exacerbated the retention problem by bringing in exactly the users least likely to stay.
Most fixes applied to the wrong constraint exacerbate the thing they were meant to help.
entries.note: Only for things already going badly. You can't exacerbate a good situation, though people write it that way constantly.

entries.definition: To reduce the severity of something without removing it.
examples: We can't eliminate platform risk, but we mitigate it by holding no more than 60% of output on any single channel.
Mitigation accepts that the bad thing happens and makes it smaller.
A mitigation plan that requires nothing to go wrong isn't a mitigation plan.
entries.note: Often confused with “militate,” which means to weigh against something. Different words, and the mix-up is common enough to notice.

entries.definition: To rule something out in advance by making it impossible.
examples: Signing an exclusive precludes the multi-brand strategy we spent last quarter arguing for, so the decision is bigger than the contract.
Nothing about a small budget precludes a good campaign; it precludes a lazy one.
Every commitment precludes something, and naming what is how you make the tradeoff visible.
entries.note: Stronger than “prevent” — precluding happens beforehand, structurally. The best strategy memos state explicitly what a choice precludes.

entries.definition: Done quickly and without depth — a look rather than an examination.
examples: A cursory read of the dashboard says the campaign worked; ten minutes with the cohort view says it pulled forward demand.
Cursory review is fine for low-stakes work and dangerous when it's the only review.
Even a cursory competitive check would have caught that the name was taken.
entries.note: Not automatically a criticism — matching depth of review to stakes is a real skill. It's only a flaw when the stakes were high.

entries.definition: Based on what was observed or measured, rather than on theory or intuition.
examples: The empirical answer is that our best-performing hook is a question, across 340 videos and four quarters.
Empirical beats plausible, and plausible beats confident.
An empirical claim comes with a sample size or it isn't one.
entries.note: Pairs directly against anecdotal. The best growth writing is explicit about which of the two it's offering.

entries.definition: Based on individual stories rather than systematic evidence.
examples: This is anecdotal, but three creators unprompted said the same thing about the brief template — worth checking properly.
Anecdotal evidence is a great source of hypotheses and a terrible source of conclusions.
The plural of anecdote isn't data, though it is usually where the data starts.
entries.note: Flagging your own evidence as anecdotal buys enormous credibility. It tells the reader you know the difference and aren't hiding it.

entries.definition: Holding a position as unquestionable, regardless of evidence.
examples: I was dogmatic about never paying per-view and the data eventually made me wrong in two specific cases.
Dogmatic beliefs are efficient — they save you from re-deciding — right up until conditions change.
The difference between principles and dogma is whether anything could revise them.
entries.note: The self-check that matters: name what evidence would change your mind. If nothing would, you're being dogmatic.

entries.definition: Impossible to stop or divert — proceeding regardless of anyone's preference.
examples: The shift of trust from institutions to individuals looks inexorable; the only open question is who intermediates it.
Rising CPMs on any platform that finds product-market fit with advertisers are inexorable, not a phase.
Calling something inexorable is a strong claim — it means planning around it rather than against it.
entries.note: Reach for it when the strategic point is adaptation rather than resistance. Overuse makes you sound like a keynote.

entries.definition: Regularly found within a particular group or place — built into the environment rather than visiting it.
examples: Late briefs are endemic to creator ops; the fix is a system that assumes them, not a reminder that scolds about them.
Survivorship bias is endemic to startup content — you only ever read the companies that made it.
Endemic problems need design changes; epidemic ones need a response.
entries.note: Distinct from epidemic (spreading fast) and pandemic (spreading everywhere). Endemic means it lives there permanently.

entries.definition: Idealistic to the point of being impractical — noble and unlikely to work.
examples: Trying to build a finance brand without ever simplifying anything is quixotic; some compression is the price of reaching people.
There's a quixotic streak in every founder, and it's load-bearing about a third of the time.
The quixotic version of a plan is often the honest one with no budget attached.
entries.note: From Don Quixote, tilting at windmills. Carries affection alongside the criticism, which is what makes it usable about people you like.

entries.definition: Impossible to see into or understand from outside.
examples: The algorithm is opaque, so we treat it empirically: change one variable, ship 20 videos, read the results.
Opaque pricing is a design choice, and customers read it correctly every time.
An opaque process inside a team produces exactly the politics you'd expect.
entries.note: Antonym of transparent, and useful about systems, pricing, and prose alike. Opaque writing is usually protecting something.

entries.definition: Genuinely relevant to the matter at hand — connected, not merely nearby.
examples: The competitor's funding round is interesting; it isn't germane to whether our creator retainers should go up.
Half of what gets raised in a strategy meeting is true, related, and not germane.
Ask whether a point is germane before arguing with it — most tangents die politely at that question.
entries.note: Sharper than “relevant” because it implies a real connection to the decision being made. A quiet way to redirect a meeting.

entries.definition: Holding two opposing feelings at once — pulled both ways, not indifferent.
examples: I'm ambivalent about the exclusive: it protects our best creator and it teaches the roster that leverage gets rewarded.
Ambivalent doesn't mean you don't care, it means you can see both sides and both are real.
Writing out the ambivalence is often how you find the decision.
entries.note: Commonly misused as “unbothered.” The prefix is ambi-, both — the whole point is that you feel two things, strongly.

entries.definition: Having no personal stake in the outcome, and therefore able to judge it fairly.
examples: We need a disinterested read on the incrementality test — anyone who owns the channel can't be the one grading it.
A fiduciary is required to be disinterested in exactly this sense.
Disinterested judgment is rare and valuable; uninterested judgment is neither.
entries.note: Not the same as uninterested (bored). Using it correctly is a small, real signal — and the distinction is genuinely useful in any review process.
